name: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
description: Interfaces should minimize irrelevant or competing information so important content and actions remain salient. In Nielsen's sense, this is mainly a clutter-reduction principle, not the separate claim that beauty itself automatically makes things more usable.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to crowded dashboards, overstuffed forms, modal-heavy flows, settings screens, landing pages with too many competing calls to action, and design-system decisions about information density.
prevalence_note: Minimalism/simplicity is one of the most pervasive norms in interface design, and Nielsen's exact heuristic remains standard in usability-review checklists even when teams shorten it to 'keep the UI clean.'

findings.description: A heuristic evaluation of 36 mobile health apps in Bangladesh found 'aesthetic and minimalist design' was the single most-violated Nielsen usability heuristic (21% of catastrophic/major usability problems), and a separate 30-participant user study found apps with more heuristic violations scored lower on the System Usability Scale -- real-world correlational evidence linking minimalist-design violations to measured usability outcomes, complementing lab-controlled clutter research with a real-world app-auditing angle.
findings.effect_size: 21% of catastrophic/major usability problems attributed to aesthetic-and-minimalist-design violations
findings.source_title: Investigating usability of mobile health applications in Bangladesh
findings.source_venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making

findings.description: Excess and/or disorganized display items produce crowding, masking, poorer recognition, and more difficult visual search; across several tested clutter measures, visual-clutter scores correlated well with both subjective clutter judgments and search performance in complex imagery. This is direct peer-reviewed support for the clutter-reduction side of minimalist UI guidance.

applications.title: 16Personalities.com: visually dense, yet satisfying the minimalist-design heuristic
applications.description: In contrast to the minimalist visual trend, 16Personalities.com uses a highly textured, information-dense visual style with little whitespace -- yet NN/g cites it as satisfying the actual aesthetic-and-minimalist-design heuristic, since it includes only necessary information rather than irrelevant noise, including on its information-dense mobile version with bottom navigation and layered progress indicators.
applications.ethical_note: Included deliberately as a counterweight to the HelloBar example in this same wave: it shows the heuristic honestly cuts both ways -- a visually 'busy' design can still be genuinely usable if every element carries real informational value, avoiding the trap of treating 'minimalist-looking' and 'satisfies the heuristic' as synonyms.

applications.title: HelloBar's homepage: minimalist style without the necessary information
applications.description: NN/g's own critique: HelloBar's homepage is extremely minimalist in visual style, but does not clearly communicate what the company does or which features are available -- an example of following the minimalist visual trend without satisfying the actual heuristic, which requires that necessary information be present and findable, not merely that the design look sparse.
applications.ethical_note: This is a structural usability critique -- a minimalist visual style that omits information users need -- not a persuasion or dark-pattern case. NN/g's own framing treats it as an unintentional side effect of chasing a visual trend rather than a deliberate withholding of information, so there is no persuasion dimension to weigh here.
